item.title: Using Batchlark
item.description:
What you are observing

Batchlark is the retained concurrency study formerly called Queue Lab/Hermes. It is not a differentiated service; a practical science-oriented replacement is being evaluated. Its dashboard represents simulated 50 ms work, not real email, webhook or language-model deliveries. It retains state in memory and resets on restart.

Run it locally

Follow the tested source setup in the implementation notes . The served application uses Go and opens a dashboard on port 8080 by default. No API key or database is needed.

item.title: Batchlark: the retained study and replacement decision
item.description:
The actual starting point

The old repository mixed early RAG scaffolding with a later webhook/concurrency demonstration. Surviving original history is:

Commit Actual historical purpose
431b89e Initial project
01e0a92 Render binding/missing-key repair
acb9d80 Rewrite toward a webhook dispatcher UI
52b6258 SSE and unit-test work

The later reviewed working tree had already repaired bounded admission, worker accounting, shutdown and slow-stream behavior, while making clear that task delivery was simulated. It was preserved as checkpoint ce80475 before this cleanup. That checkpoint records pre-existing work, not newly invented development.

item.title: Running the queue simulation
item.description:
Status: retained engineering exercise; a practical replacement is being evaluated. This is the former Queue Lab/Hermes implementation. A worker pool alone is not a differentiated service, and this project is not presented as a paid SaaS or production queue.

What is implemented

  • Fifty fixed Go workers and a bounded 10,000-task queue.
  • Whole-batch admission with HTTP 429/Retry-After under pressure.
  • Strict JSON/body/count validation, bounded retained batches and event subscribers.
  • JSON metrics, batch status and server-sent progress events; slow consumers disconnect.
  • Graceful shutdown drains accepted simulated work.
  • A browser dashboard with bounded recent events and polling recovery.

Tasks simulate a 50 ms delay. No webhook, LLM, scientific computation or paid customer work is performed. State is in memory and disappears on restart. The simulation is useful for studying concurrency mechanics, not evidence of durable delivery or production throughput.
